chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abi Basir, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said:

He was asked about a boy who had not reached maturity and a woman who killed a man by mistake, so he said: "Indeed, the mistaken killing of the woman and the boy is treated as intentional. If the heirs of the slain wish to kill them both, they may kill them both, and they must return to the heirs of the boy five thousand dirhams. And if they wish to kill the boy, they may kill him, and the woman must return to the heirs of the boy one quarter of the blood-money."
He said: "And if the heirs of the slain wish to take the blood-money, then half of the blood-money is upon the boy and half of the blood-money is upon the woman."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: I have cited these two narrations because of what they contain of the rulings of intentional killing. As for his statement in the first report, "the mistake of the woman and the slave is intentional," and in the other narration, "the mistake of the woman and the boy is intentional," this contradicts the saying of Allah, the Exalted, because Allah has ruled blood-money rather than retaliation in mistaken killing. So it is not permissible for mistake to be intentional, just as it is not permissible for intentional killing to be mistaken killing, except in the case of one who is not legally responsible, such as the insane and those who are not rational. Also, we have previously presented reports indicating that if a slave kills by mistake, he is handed over to the heirs of the slain, or his master redeems him, and they do not have the right to kill him. Likewise, we have explained that if a child has not reached maturity, then his intentional act is mistaken killing, and his 'aqilah bears the blood-money. So how can it be permissible for us to say in this narration that his mistake is intentional? And if the two reports are as we have said, affected by confusion, then it is not proper to act upon them in what pertains to treating mistake as intentional. However, it appears that the meaning may be that their mistake is intentional according to what some of our opponents regard as mistaken, because among them are those who say that everyone who kills without an iron weapon, then his killing is mistaken. We have already explained the contrary to that, and that killing by any thing whatsoever, if intended, is intentional. And the meaning of his statement عليه السلام, 'a boy who had not reached,' is that he had not reached the limit of completion, because we have already explained that when he reaches five spans, retaliation is carried out against him.

key_terms.أَوْلِيَاءُ الْمَقْتُولِ: the heirs or legal representatives of the slain person
key_terms.اقْتُصَّ: retaliation was carried out; legal retribution applied
key_terms.الدِّيَةِ: blood-money; financial compensation due in cases of killing
key_terms.الْقَوَدِ: retaliatory execution or legal retaliation in homicide
key_terms.خَطَأً: mistakenly; accidental killing as opposed to deliberate intent
key_terms.عَاقِلَتُهُ: his 'aqilah; the agnatic group that bears liability for blood-money
key_terms.عَمْدٌ: intentional; deliberate killing that normally entails retaliation
key_terms.غُلَامٍ: a boy; here, a young male discussed in relation to legal responsibility

ai.seo_question: How does Tahdhib al-Ahkam address a narration that seems to treat mistaken killing by a woman or boy as intentional?
ai.summary: This report discusses the legal ruling concerning a woman and an underage boy involved in mistaken killing, followed by Shaykh al-Tusi's analysis of the report. He explains that the wording treating mistaken killing as intentional conflicts with the established ruling that mistaken killing entails blood-money rather than retaliation, and he clarifies how the narration may be understood or why it should not be acted upon in that literal sense.
